Knowledge distillation is a technique used to train compact, high-performing models, achieving results comparable to larger models while consuming significantly less computational resources. The key concept involves training a small model to mimic a large model's performance. However, existing approaches require access to the large model's parameters throughout training to calculate the loss functions, limiting its efficiency. Our proposed solution, Distiller, addresses this limitation by developing a separate module capable of estimating the large model's performance given a set of large model checkpoints. This enables the distiller to be trained independently and efficiently use a range of large models as a supervisory signal to train multiple small models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Distiller in training SqueezeNet models that match ResNet-101 performance on ImageNet while using just 0.01% of its parameters, and also show its applicability in training models from pre-trained large models like BERT. Ultimately, this capability to rapidly simulate wildfire behavior across diverse scenarios has the potential to significantly enhance policymakers' and decision-makers' ability to respond to the growing threat of wildfires. This paper details progress on developing a natural language generation system as part of the EU-funded research project, ArgumenTator.  The ultimate goal of this initiative is to create a legal expert system capable of offering informed opinions on complex legal matters in Europe. To achieve this objective, ArguenTator is based on a rule-based approach that incorporates machine learning and natural language generation. To provide informed advice, the system needs to distill relevant information from vast legal databases and generate coherent, understandable output. To accomplish this, the paper describes a pipeline that extracts relevant legal knowledge from databases and uses that information to produce natural language arguments supporting a specific legal conclusion. Furthermore, the paper discusses a method to automatically determine the most relevant knowledge artifacts for a specific legal conclusion. To complete the system, the paper also outlines a natural language generator that takes a set of knowledge artifacts and a legal conclusion as input and produces a natural language argument. To demonstrate the system's capabilities, the paper includes examples of generated legal arguments. Despite the system's limitations, preliminary results indicate its potential in offering informed legal advice. To facilitate further research, the paper provides access to the knowledge artifacts and an initial working prototype. To view the system in action, an online demo is available on the project's website. Finally, this paper discusses ongoing and future research directions in the ArguenTator project. Highly accurate hyperspectral images are crucial for a range of applications, 
but noise within the images can severely impair performance.  Consequently, 
hyperspectral image denoising has become a pressing research priority. 
Unfortunately, the complex relationships between different spectral bands in 
these images make it difficult to develop effective denoising techniques. 
Recently, researchers have explored the use of attention mechanisms to 
overcome this challenge, but existing approaches have been limited by their 
failure to fully account for relationships between spectral bands. 
To address this issue, we introduce a new method called the spatial-spectral 
cross attention network (SSCAN), designed to denoise hyperspectral images. 
Our innovative method enables the network to capture relationships between 
different spectral bands by considering the spatial context of each band. 
Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of SSCAN and its ability 
to outperform existing state-of-the-art techniques. The implementation of 
SSCAN will be made publicly available. The associated code can be found at 
https://github.com/ChangshengGao/SSCAN. Further information can be found at 
https://doi.org/10.1109/L-ISP.2022Sterc.26805.

Constructing accurate cost values is a crucial step in light field depth estimation. However, current methods typically employ a basic image matching cost constructor, which may lead to suboptimal results due to occlusion. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel cost constructor that incorporates multi-view information to mitigate occlusion. This new constructor is divided into two components: the first estimates depth values based on a reference image's parallax, while the second identifies occluded areas by analyzing disparities among views. To further enhance performance, we also propose a method to combine depth values and a cost function that takes occlusion into account.
